opus-5.5.text:
I think for me, the key is that I don't really treat setbacks as something separate from the long-term path. They're part of it. When you work on something like machine learning systems, which is what I've been doing for a long time, almost nothing works the first time. With XGBoost, with TVM, with a lot of the projects my collaborators and I have done, there were many moments where the benchmark numbers didn't look good, or people didn't see why we were doing it, or a paper got rejected. If you only measure yourself by those short-term signals, it's very easy to get discouraged.

So one thing that helps me is to anchor on the problem rather than the outcome. I ask myself: do I still believe this problem matters? Do I still believe that, say, making machine learning run efficiently everywhere is going to be important five or ten years from now? If the answer is yes, then a setback just tells me something about *how* I'm approaching it, not *whether* I should keep going. That reframing makes it much easier to keep moving.

The second thing is to break the long-term goal into small things I can actually enjoy day to day. I genuinely like writing code, I like debugging, I like seeing a system get a little faster. If you only get satisfaction from the big milestone at the end, you're going to have a hard time, because the big milestones are rare. But if you can find joy in the small progress, then long-termism isn't really a sacrifice anymore. It's just what you're doing every day.

And the third thing, honestly, is people. Open source has taught me a lot about this. When you build something together with a community, you're not carrying everything alone. There are days when I'm tired or a direction isn't working, and someone else in the community comes up with an idea or fixes something, and that keeps the momentum going. Having students and collaborators who share the same vision makes the setbacks feel much lighter.

So I'd say it's a mix of believing in the problem, enjoying the process, and having good people around you. Setbacks still hurt, of course. But over time you learn that they are usually temporary, and the things that compound are the ones you kept doing anyway.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that I don't treat setbacks as evidence against the long-term direction. I treat them as information about the path.

When we were building XGBoost, or later TVM and MLC, there were long stretches where things just didn't work. A kernel would be slower than the baseline for weeks. A design that felt elegant on paper would fall apart on real hardware. Early on, that's painful, because you start to wonder whether the whole bet was wrong. What helped me was separating two questions. One is, is the destination still right? The other is, is this particular step right? Most setbacks only answer the second question. The destination, something like making machine learning deployable anywhere, on any hardware, through open source, that doesn't change because one compiler pass failed.

The second thing is that I try to find a unit of progress that is small enough to see every week. If your only measure is the five-year vision, you'll be discouraged constantly, because by that measure you're always behind. But if you can say, this week the operator fused correctly, or this week one more person got their model running on their laptop, then you have a steady stream of real wins. Those small wins compound, and they also keep you honest, because they're concrete.

And then there's community. A lot of what I do is open source, and the people around a project carry it through the moments when any single person would give up. Someone files a bug, someone else fixes it, a student uses it in a way you never expected. That reminds you the thing exists outside your own head. It's not just your commitment anymore. That shared ownership is probably the strongest form of long-termism I know. It outlasts anyone's bad month.

So, to put it simply, I keep the long goal fixed, I let the path be flexible, I look for small visible progress, and I don't try to do it alone.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficult part is separating commitment to a goal from commitment to a particular approach. You can believe that a problem matters over the long term and still accept that your current approach isn’t working.

When setbacks happen, I try to make the question smaller: What did we learn? What assumption needs to change? What can we try next? If you judge every day by whether you’ve reached a ten-year goal, most days will feel disappointing. But if you can see that you understand the problem better, that gives you a reason to continue.

And long-termism shouldn’t mean continuing blindly. You need to revisit why the work matters. If that reason still holds, then a setback can change the route without changing the destination.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, long-term commitment doesn’t mean being certain that every step will work. It means having a direction that I care about, while being willing to change how I get there.

When something fails, I try to make the question smaller: What did we learn? What can we try next? A setback can feel overwhelming if you treat it as a judgment on the whole journey. It becomes more manageable when it gives you information about the next step.

And I think sustainability matters. You need small signs of progress, people you can learn with, and time to recover. You can be patient about the long-term outcome while still being very concrete about what you do today.
